activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
The argument started over a dented trash can lid, which Daniel thought was a strange thing for two best friends to fight about. He had come to Blaine's house to work on their science project, but instead he was standing in the kitchen watching Blaine and Lorelai glare at each other across the counter.

"He slammed it on purpose," Lorelai said. "You were mad about the group grade and you took it out on my project."

"I set it down and it rolled off the table," Blaine said. "You just assume the worst because you're still sore about the grade."

"You're the one being unreasonable."

Daniel remembered the previous Saturday, when he had watched the whole thing happen from the porch. Blaine had been carrying an armful of display boards, and the lid had slid off the pile when he turned too fast. He hadn't even been looking at it. But when Daniel said, "I saw it, it was an accident," Lorelai just folded her arms, and Blaine muttered, "See? Even Daniel agrees with me," which somehow made everything worse.

Daniel retreated to the living room, where Blaine's older sister was doing homework at the coffee table. He asked her how two people could watch the same trash can lid and see two different events. She slid a psych textbook across the couch toward him without looking up. "It's called naive realism," she said, and went back to her notes.

He read the page twice. Naive realism was the belief that we see the world as it really is, so anyone who disagrees with us must be uninformed or biased. Lorelai wasn't lying and Blaine wasn't lying. Each of them was certain the truth was obvious, and each one decided the other was the problem. Daniel set the book down and thought about his plan for the science project, which involved testing an idea you couldn't see directly. You could do that with people, too.

He marched back into the kitchen and made them each a vigorous argument for the opposite side, Blaine's accident story delivered to Lorelai, Lorelai's motive theory delivered to Blaine. Then he offered a treaty: they would both participate in rebuilding the display for the class presentation, and nobody had to admit anything about the lid.

Lorelai was the first to crack a smile. "You're saying we're both sure we're right, and both positive the other one is being ridiculous."

"That's exactly what I'm saying," said Daniel, and handed her a glue stick.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
story:
Muhammad had agreed to babysit for Ms. Katz mostly because she paid ten dollars an hour and mostly because he wanted the money before Saturday. The plan seemed simple: watch the baby, feed the baby, keep the baby alive until Ms. Katz got home at nine. The whole evening, he discovered, would revolve around a small person named Rose who could not say a single word but had strong opinions anyway.

Ms. Katz's son Zack was supposed to be at his friend's house, but his friend got sick, so Zack was there too, lying on the couch with a comic and pretending he did not need a babysitter. He was eight. Muhammad decided not to argue about the chain of command.

At six o'clock Rose started making a specific sound, a cranky huh huh huh that Muhammad quickly learned was her signal for hunger. He found the jar of baby oatmeal on the counter and the note Ms. Katz had left taped to the fridge. He mixed the cereal with warm water, tested it on his wrist like she'd shown him, and offered the spoon. Rose clamped her mouth shut. He tried again. She turned her whole face away, which for someone who could not sit up on her own was a fairly clear statement.

Muhammad looked around the kitchen for ideas. On the shelf above the stove sat a bear-shaped bottle of honey, and he remembered his own mother stirring a spoonful into his little brother's tea when the boy had a sore throat. Sweet things made food better. He reached for the bottle.

"You can't," Zack said, not even looking up from his comic.

"Why not?"

Zack pointed the corner of his comic at the fridge note. Muhammad leaned in and read the part he had skipped, the part in capital letters. NO HONEY. He read it twice. Babies under twelve months should never have honey, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.

"Huh," Muhammad said. He set the bear down on the shelf, feeling as though he had almost done something without ever knowing it was a something.

"So she hates the oatmeal," he said. "What do we do?"

"Try it warmer," Zack said. "Mom heats it up more than that. She says it's a thing."

Muhammad tested his theory. He warmed the bowl another thirty seconds, offered the spoon again, and Rose opened her mouth like a small pink trapdoor and ate the entire serving. When Ms. Katz came home, she found the kitchen clean, the baby asleep, and Zack taking full credit for the temperature.

"He was going to use the honey," Zack announced.

Ms. Katz looked at Muhammad. Muhammad held up the empty oatmeal jar. "Read the note twice," he said. "That's the whole job."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and the folding chairs were arranged in rows facing a low stage where Ms. Gauthier sat with a stack of index cards. Kaylee sat in the third row between Victor and Alisa, her number pinned to her shirt, waiting for her turn in the school spelling bee. The winner would retrieve the district trophy from the front office cabinet, where it had sat since last year, and Kaylee wanted it.

Words came and went. Victor spelled "nutritious" correctly, and Alisa went out on "salmon." Then Ms. Gauthier called Kaylee's word. "Chorus. It comes from Greek." Kaylee froze. She heard a k sound at the start, but k could be spelled several ways. Then she thought about "chef," which Alisa's grandmother, who was proud of her French heritage, said all the time. In "chef" the sh sound came from French. This word was Greek, not French. She remembered her word list at home, the Greek column, where k sounds kept showing up as "ch." She decided to test that pattern right now.

"Chorus. C-H-O-R-U-S. Chorus."

"Correct," said Ms. Gauthier.

Two rounds later, only Kaylee and a seventh grader were left. The seventh grader stepped up, and Ms. Gauthier read the next card. "Chef. The language of origin is French." The seventh grader frowned. "C-H-E-F," he said slowly. "Wait. C-H-E..." He stopped, started over, and spelled it with a k at the end. The buzzer sounded.

Ms. Gauthier turned to Kaylee for the winning word. "There's a word on this card I wasn't planning to use until the district bee," she said, almost apologetic. "Monarch. It comes to us through French."

Kaylee's mouth went dry. The middle of it had that k sound. She had just watched French break her pattern in front of everyone, because in "chef" the special spelling was the sh, and the k sound in "monarch" might follow some rule she didn't know. She stood at the microphone while the whole gym waited.

"M-O-N-A-R-C-H. Monarch."

Ms. Gauthier looked at the card, then at her, and reached slowly for the buzzer.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
The problem sat in the middle of Gavin's kitchen table like a dare: an assignment sheet from Ms. Kapoor that said, Explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and you must use a primary source. He had his textbook open, and the textbook had a whole chapter on the westward movement, but every time he tried to start his paragraph, the assignment sheet seemed to stare back at him.

He called Lydia first. "What does primary even mean?" he asked. "The textbook is, like, the main book."

"Wait, I think my sister did this," Lydia said. "Hold on." He heard her shouting upstairs, then she came back breathless. "Okay, a primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through it. Like a settler's diary. And a secondary source is written later by someone studying it."

Gavin looked at his textbook, which was printed three years ago about events from two hundred years ago. His stomach did a slow flip, the same one he'd felt in fourth grade when he realized he'd been feeding the class hamster twice a day and nobody else was feeding it at all. He had been about to write his whole report on a secondary source. He closed the textbook with a thud.

Sia arrived with her backpack and a folder of printouts. "The library had scanned pages online," she said, spreading them across the table so they covered the wood, the smell of the printer's warm ink still rising off them. "Diaries from people on the trail. Some are hard to read."

Gavin leaned over a page where faded ink had saturated the paper until the letters bled into each other. He squinted at one entry, sounding it out: "June the third. The mule is lame and we have only half the flour we left with, and still my husband insists we go on, for the land in Oregon is said to be free to any who will work it."

"That's a reason," Sia said, tapping the page. "The land. And the mule thing, that's what it cost them."

"Ms. Kapoor said the most influential details are the ones that show why," Gavin said slowly, "not just what happened." He tested it out on another diary, an 1852 entry from a woman describing a lawyer she'd met on the trail who kept a list of every family passing his camp. A lawyer counting families, families who had left schools and shops and colleagues behind in Missouri. That was a pattern he couldn't see directly, but here it was in ink: people had whole lives already, and they left them anyway, for land.

He opened a blank document and typed the first sentence: A settler's diary shows why families moved west, even when the trip nearly broke them.

"There," Sia said.

He read the June third entry one more time, then started typing the second sentence.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A traditional formal outline labels main points with Roman numerals such as I, II and III, and the details under each point with capital letters such as A and B.
story:
Mr. Goldberg made outlines mandatory before anyone wrote a single word of the persuasive essay, and he had taped a sample outline to the board at the front of Room 12. Bentley stared at it while the radiator ticked and the smell of chalk dust settled over the desks. His topic was due by the end of the period, and the sheet in front of him was still blank except for his name.

He wanted to argue that the school should keep its old oak tree instead of cutting it down for the new parking lot. He knew what he felt about it. What he did not know was how to squeeze a whole argument into one sentence at the top of the page, the way Mr. Goldberg kept asking for.

Kaden leaned over from the next desk. "Why do the numbers on that thing look like the ones on a clock?" he whispered. "Is that a three, or a weird letter?"

Bentley looked again. The sample outline had a I, a II, and a III marching down the left side, each marking one of the three main points, and under each main point sat a capital A and a capital B for the details. It was strange, but the strange parts were orderly. The big points got the clock-like numbers. The smaller stuff got plain letters.

He tried it himself. At the top he wrote his one sentence: the school should save the oak tree because it shades the building, it is home to birds, and it is older than the school itself. That was the whole argument folded flat, like a map. Then he wrote I and put the shading point next to it, with A for the afternoon temperature readings Mr. Goldberg had let the class take outside last week, and B for the shade over the benches where kids ate lunch. II got the birds, with A for the nest Anabel had photographed in May and B for the list of species the class had counted. III got the age, with A for the date on the old photograph in the hallway and B for the ring count the principal had mentioned.

It was like testing a rule. If the outline held together, he could write the essay straight down the page, point by point, and nothing would wander. He slid the paper toward Anabel, who sat in front of him. "Does this demonstrate that I actually have a plan, or does it just look like one?"

She read it upside down for a second, then turned around and took it properly. "It's a plan. Each point has its own evidence under it. Also, that part about the benches is good, it's like a simile without actually being one, the tree doing the protecting."

Mr. Goldberg walked the rows, pausing at desks, nodding at some papers and tapping others. When he reached Bentley, he read the outline all the way through, both hands in his pockets. "Roman numerals and letters, in the right places," he said. "And a thesis that actually makes a claim. Start drafting."

Bentley picked up his pen and wrote his first sentence, following the map he had just drawn.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
Michael stood at the edge of the drama room carpet, chewing the inside of his cheek. Ms. Campbell had written two words on the board: yes, and. Their assignment was to improvise a scene with a partner, and in one hour they would perform in front of the whole class. His partner was Yohan, who was already pacing and muttering to himself, because Yohan wanted the lead in the spring play and believed this class was his audition.

They tried a practice scene on the spot. "Welcome aboard," Michael said, steadying an imaginary wheel. "The sea is rough tonight."

"We're not on a boat," Yohan said. "This is a cafeteria."

Michael felt the scene drop like a cut string. He had nowhere to go. The floor was just a floor again. They tried twice more, and both times Yohan denied whatever Michael offered, and both times the scene died before it started. "It's like you're slamming a door," Michael said. Reagan, who was practicing nearby, looked over. "In drama that's called blocking," she said. "You reject or ignore what your partner gives you, and it stops the scene from moving forward."

Michael turned the idea over. Nobody could see a rule like that; it was invisible until you broke it. But he had watched it happen three times in a row, so he decided to test it. "One more," he said. "Whatever I say, don't deny it. Build on it. Yes, and."

Yohan rubbed the back of his neck. "Fine. But if you make me a talking sheep, I quit."

"Welcome aboard," Michael said again. "The sea is rough tonight."

"Yes," Yohan said, slow at first, "and the captain lost his hat overboard."

"And the hat," Michael said, "was a gift from my grandmother, who happens to be a shark."

Yohan laughed, a real one, and then leaned into the wheel like a man fighting waves. Suddenly they had a grandmother shark, a hat, and a storm, all of it invented out of nothing. Michael could feel the difference, like current in a wire. When Ms. Campbell clapped and called time, Yohan was still grinning.

Later, while the class lined up, Yohan slid next to Michael. "The thing is," he said quietly, "I kept saying no because I thought whoever controlled the setting would look like the leader. That was dumb. It was arbitrary, like deciding the scene by coin flip." Michael shrugged. "You didn't look like a leader. You looked like a guy in a cafeteria arguing about a boat." Yohan winced, then laughed. When their turn came, they stood back to back, and Michael opened his palms like a book. "Ready to hear the strangest library rule ever?"

"Rules are eroding everywhere, my friend," Yohan said, "and this library is next."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A formula that includes its own cell, such as =SUM(B2:B10) typed into cell B10, is called a circular reference, and Excel warns about it.
story:
Kaylee sat cross-legged on the floor of Genesis's bedroom with a laptop balanced on a binder, because Genesis's desk was buried under laundry and half a model volcano. On the screen was a spreadsheet of their science-class fundraiser: thirty rows of candy sales, one column for the money each student brought in. If they could total it and turn it into a bar chart before Monday, Mr. Holloway would let them present the results to the whole class. Kaylee wanted that more than she had wanted anything since the audition for jazz band.

"Type the total here," Genesis said, pointing at a blank cell near the bottom of the numbers. Kaylee scrolled, picked a spot, and entered =SUM(B2:B10). She pressed Enter.

The screen flickered and a warning box appeared, gray and sudden, with an exclamation mark inside a diamond. Kaylee's stomach dropped. "What did I do?"

Genesis leaned over her shoulder, which only seemed to magnify the problem, since now two people were staring at a message neither of them understood. "It says something about a circular reference," Genesis read slowly. "What is that?"

Kaylee looked at the cell where she had typed the formula. Then she looked up at the formula bar, and her eyes moved between them twice. She had entered the sum in cell B10, the very last cell in the range she was adding. The formula was adding up B2 through B10, and it was sitting inside B10, trying to add itself. She could not see the machine thinking, but she could see the pattern, like guessing there was a wire crossed behind a wall.

"Wait," she said. "I think I get it. It's in its own sum. It's eating its own tail." She deleted the formula, moved down one row to B11, and typed =SUM(B2:B10) again. The warning did not come back. In its place sat a number, the whole fundraiser total, plain as anything.

"It worked," Genesis said, and Kaylee laughed so loudly that a spontaneous round of applause broke out from the doorway, where Leslie had been watching the whole time with a bag of chips.

"Chart time," Kaylee said, and highlighted the column. "Mr. Holloway is going to lose his mind."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
The banners at the cultural center were so orange they made Alexander squint, which was saying something, because he had spent the whole drive here squinting at his little sister's karaoke. His father had been hired to transport the sound equipment for the Vaisakhi celebration, and Alexander had been dragged along to carry cables. His friends Iris and Charles had come too, mostly for the food, though Charles claimed he was there "for cultural research," which meant he wanted to watch the drummers.

"So what's the big deal about today?" Charles asked, nodding at the stage where a man in a bright turban was testing a microphone. "Is it like a harvest thing? My mom said something about harvest."

"That's what I thought," Alexander said. "But look." He pointed at a long banner near the entrance. It showed a painted scene of a crowd gathered around one man on a hillside, and the crowd looked serious, not harvest-y at all. Nobody carries swords to a wheat festival, Alexander reasoned, unless it is a very strange wheat festival. He decided to test his harvest theory. "If it's just harvest, there'll be wheat everywhere. Let's count the wheat."

They counted. Iris found wheat on one poster, painted behind some dancing figures. Charles found wheat in a mural, small and golden in the corner. But in the middle of the mural stood a man raising a sword, and around him, five figures. No wheat touched them at all. Alexander's harvest theory was wobbling like Charles after the merry-go-round incident in third grade.

"Okay, new plan," Alexander said. "We find someone who actually knows and we eavesdrop politely."

"Eavesdrop politely," Iris repeated. "That's called listening."

They drifted toward the food tables, where a girl about seven was tugging her uncle's sleeve. "Why does this day matter so much?" she asked. "Everybody keeps saying Vaisakhi, Vaisakhi."

Her uncle smiled and crouched down. "It's the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," he said. "That's the story those banners are showing. That's why this day matters."

Alexander felt like a locker had swung open in his brain. Not harvest. A founding. The swords, the five figures, the crowd on the hill, all of it clicked into place like the last piece of a puzzle, except the puzzle had been hiding under the table the whole time.

Charles raised his hand as if in class. "So when we eat the food, are we honoring the Khalsa or the wheat?"

"Both," the uncle said, laughing. "The wheat doesn't mind sharing."

A drummer hit a deep, buoyant boom that rattled the juice cups, and Iris grabbed both boys by the sleeves. The procession was forming near the stage, orange flags lifting like small sails, and the three of them dove into the crowd just as the drums rolled forward.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Michael sat at the kitchen table with a photocopy of "The Scarlet Ibis" by James Hurst, a story from 1960 that Mr. Mercer had assigned on Tuesday. The quiz was tomorrow, and Michael had read the thing twice without knowing what he was supposed to see in it. He slid the pages around, read the part about the red bird again, and dragged his chair over to the laptop to message Bethany.

"Did you figure out what Mercer wants us to notice?" he typed.

She answered with a shrug emoji, which helped nobody. Michael frowned at the page. In the story, a storm had blown a red bird into the family's garden, and the bird died there. Then the story went on about Doodle, a fragile boy, and Michael had a feeling the bird was not just a bird. He began to speculate. Maybe the dead bird was a hint about what would happen to Doodle a few pages later. He checked the last page first, which felt like cheating, and then he saw it: Doodle's fate matched the bird's. The bird had come before, the way a weather report comes before rain.

He tried the idea out like a mechanism, turning it over. The author could not just come out and say what would happen, so he put a signpost in early. It was like the birds that used to flock over the fields near his grandfather's town and were now extinct; people knew something was wrong only because of what they noticed and remembered. If you paid attention to the pattern, you could see what was coming.

Bethany showed up at four with her own photocopy, wrinkled from her backpack, and a bag of chips she did not share. "Jules says the bird is just there to be sad," she said, dropping into the other chair.

"Then why is it red? Why does a storm blow it in? Why is it in the garden, of all places?" Michael tapped the page. "The bird dies in the garden. Then look what happens to Doodle. It's a setup. The first thing tells you about the second thing."

Bethany read the ending, chewed a chip, and read it again. "Okay," she said. "That's creepy and also kind of great. What do we call it, though? Mercer will want the word."

Michael scrolled through his notes until he found the term from Monday's class. "Foreshadowing. The bird foreshadows what happens to Doodle." He wrote it in his notebook, then wrote the sentence again in case the first one looked accidental.

They drilled each other until dinner. Bethany quizzed him on the year, the author, the bird, the garden, the storm, and Michael got them all right, even upside down with his eyes closed, which he demonstrated and immediately regretted when he knocked his water onto the photocopy. He dried it with a paper towel, and the red bird on the page smeared into a pink blur that looked, Bethany said, like the one thing the quiz would definitely ask about.

"It's a sign," Michael said, holding it up. "Even the water is foreshadowing."

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Watercolour is transparent, so each wash lets the layers beneath show through; that is why painters work from light to dark, because a dark wash cannot be covered by a lighter one.
story:
Elena squeezed the last toothpaste-coloured ribbon out of her yellow paint tube and flattened the empty thing with her thumb, like pressing a tiny piston until nothing was left inside. Across the studio, Dakota was already halfway through her portrait, and hers looked amazing: silver hair, dark eyes, a proud grandmother staring out of the paper.

"How did you get the hair so dark already?" Elena asked.

"I did it first," Dakota said, "so I wouldn't have to fuss with it later. Now I'm adding the highlight down the middle, that bright grey streak."

Elena watched her friend load a pale wash on her brush and drag it across the dark hair. Then she watched the pale wash vanish. Dakota tried again, heavier, and again the dark swallowed it, the way a lake swallows a dropped coin. Dakota stared at her brush as if it had lied to her.

Elena looked down at her own portrait, which was barely started, just a faint peach glow where her grandfather's face would be. She had been about to jump straight to his grey beard so it would look like something. Now she paused. Something invisible was going on here. She dipped her brush in clean water and painted a square of pale yellow on scrap paper, let it dry, then brushed a darker orange over half of it. The yellow glowed up through the orange like firelight through a curtain. She tried the reverse, orange first, then yellow on top. The yellow did nothing. It was like trying to unring a bell.

"Dakota," she said slowly, "watercolour is transparent. Whatever's underneath shows through."

"So my highlight is trapped under the dark hair."

"Under, nothing. It's gone. You can't cover a dark wash with a lighter one. You have to go light to dark." Elena turned back to her grandfather and began, for the first time, in the right order. A whisper of yellow. A breath of pink for the cheeks. She layered wash after wash, each one a little deeper, and the face rose up out of the paper as though it had been hiding there all along, waiting to be let out in the correct sequence.

Outside the window, a wedge of migratory geese cut across the grey sky, headed somewhere warm. Mr. Campbell-Brown, who was retiring from the studio at the end of the month and kept saying so, wandered past with his coffee mug and stopped behind Elena's easel.

"Well," he said. "Somebody's been doing her experiments."

Behind him, Dakota flipped her paper to the blank side and started again, whispering, "Light to dark, light to dark," like a spell.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.
story:
The bus smelled like old vinyl and orange peel, and Brooke had her word list balanced on her knees, going through it for the fourth time. Sabrina sat beside her, flipping through a library book about the Scripps National Spelling Bee that she had borrowed mostly to keep Brooke company. The regional bee was in forty minutes, at the middle school across town, and Brooke's biggest rival, Aryanna, was two rows back mouthing words to herself.

"You should read this," Sabrina said, turning the book around. "In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee." Brooke looked at the photograph, a girl her own age holding a trophy nearly as tall as she was, and something in her chest shifted. She had assumed the champions were always the same kind of kid, the kind with tutors and five thousand hours of practice, but Zaila had practiced with a spreadsheet her dad made. An ordinary girl, and then not ordinary at all.

"How did she handle the hard ones?" Brooke asked. Sabrina paged backward. "It says she thought about where words come from. French words, Greek words. Each language has its own fingerprint." Brooke chewed on that. She noticed her own list had a pattern she had never seen before: the French words, like crotchet and ricochet, all ended in that soft sliding sound, while the Greek ones, like xanthoma, carried distinct clusters of letters that barely looked like English at all. Was that a real rule, or just a trick her eyes were playing?

She decided to test it. "Sabrina, quiz me on the ones I marked F." Croissant, demiurge, cortege, one after another, and every time the French spelling came out of her pencil the way it sounded, glidey and quiet. Then the Greek ones, and those she built like blocks, consonant by consonant. It held. The pattern was real, hiding inside her own list the whole time, waiting for her to notice.

The bus lurched around the last corner and shuddered to a stop in front of the other school. Aryanna was already in the aisle, so Brooke made a quick pivot into her seat to let her pass, then folded her list and slid it into her jacket pocket.

"Number forty-one," the proctor called once they were seated on the stage, and Brooke stood, straightened her card with the big 41 on it, and waited.

"Your word is mignonette," the proctor said.

"Language of origin?" Brooke asked, and when the answer came back, French, she almost smiled. "Mignonette. M-I-G-N-O-N-E-T-T-E. Mignonette."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A round-robin, in which each person speaks in turn around the circle, gives quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas.
story:
The robotics club met in the corner of the gym, ten minutes before track practice started, because Mr. Singh let them use the equipment room as long as they were gone by four o'clock. Leah stood at the front with her agenda written on the back of a race bib: fundraiser ideas, robot sensor calibration, and a decision about the competition entry. So far the meeting had gone like every other one. Lily-Anne had talked for four straight minutes about a bake sale, two boys had argued about T-shirt colours, and the clock on the wall showed 3:52.

"We still need one fundraiser idea before Mr. Singh kicks us out," Leah said. "Who's got something?"

Lily-Anne started again, something about car washes. The boys talked over her. Leah looked down the row of folding chairs and noticed Leighton, who sat by the door with his notebook closed on his knee. He had not said a word in three meetings. She had assumed he had nothing to offer, but now she thought about it differently. Maybe he had ideas and no room to fit them in. It was like a robot with a blocked sensor, she thought: the signal was there, but nothing was picking it up.

"Stop," Leah said. She held up the agenda. "We're doing it differently. It's called a round-robin. Each person speaks in turn around the circle, one at a time, and nobody talks until it's their turn."

"That's a tournament thing," Lily-Anne said.

"It works for talking too," Leah said. "Start with Leighton."

The room went quiet. Leighton opened his notebook. He had drawn the whole plan already: instead of one big fundraiser, each club member would bring a small item for a mystery-box raffle at the science night, with tickets sold at fifty cents. The boxes cost almost nothing to make, and every member could contribute without baking or washing cars. Around the circle, each person added one detail, and nobody got talked over, because the rule gave everyone a guaranteed turn.

The clock said 3:58. They voted on the raffle, and it passed with every hand up, including Leighton's.

"Time," Mr. Singh called from the gym door, whistle in hand.

Leah copied the plan into the agenda while everyone gathered their bags. Leighton stopped beside her chair on his way out.

"Same thing next meeting?" he asked.

"Round-robin," Leah said, and wrote it at the top of the page.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Islam teaches that on the Day of Judgment, called Yawm al-Qiyamah, all people will be raised and judged, and sent to paradise or hell.
story:
Lily spread her two posters across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with teacups so the summer breeze from the open window wouldn't lift them. One poster showed a single road with an arrow pointing to a gate. The other showed a wheel with spokes looping back on itself. "Grandma," she called, "can I borrow your markers? Mine died."

Her grandmother came in from the garden, brushing soil off her hands, and set a glass of lemonade beside the teacups. "What's all this, then?"

"It's my summer project," Lily said. "Mr. Lavoie asked us to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. I chose Islam and Hinduism." She uncapped the borrowed marker and drew a small scale on the first poster, trying to illustrate the idea of weighing. "Leana's family is Muslim and Koen's is Hindu, so I'm interviewing both of them tomorrow. But first I want to guess, so I can test myself."

"Test yourself how?" her grandmother asked, sitting down.

Lily tapped the wheel poster. "I know Hindus believe in many lives, like a rodent running inside a wheel, going around and around until it finally gets out." She tapped the road poster. "And I think Islam is more like this. One road, one end. But I'm not sure what's at the end. Maybe it just stops?"

She wrote her guess in the corner, small enough to cross out later. At the window, her grandmother's cat made an agile leap onto the sill and settled there to watch the teacups as if they might move.

The next morning, Leana came over with her older sister's books stacked under one arm. Lily read while Leana flipped pages and translated the parts written in Arabic. "Here," Leana said, pointing. "My sister says it's called Yawm al-Qiyamah, the Day of Judgment."

Lily wrote the words carefully. "So what happens on that day?"

"Everybody gets raised," Leana said. "All people. Then they're judged, and sent to paradise or hell."

Lily stared at the road poster, then crossed out her small corner guess and wrote beside the gate: raised, judged, paradise or hell. "So it's one life, one judgment, one final place. Not a wheel at all. The wheel and the road are like opposites."

"Kind of," Leana said, tilting her head. "Except both of them have an ending, if you think about it. The wheel stops eventually too."

Lily hadn't thought of that. She added a note in the margin, then grabbed the phone and called Koen to check whether the wheel really did stop, or whether it just kept turning forever.

"Depends who you ask," Koen said through the speaker, laughing. "Bring the posters to my place. My dad wants to see the wheel one."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
The Number 14 bus smelled like wet raincoats and orange peel, and Paisley had exactly eleven minutes to figure out why the monkey's paw mattered. Ms. Cheung had handed out the story that afternoon, and tomorrow each student had to stand up and explain one example of foreshadowing or symbolism, which meant Paisley's whole grade was riding on a shriveled little paw in a story from 1902.

"Read it out loud to me," said Inaaya, who had the window seat and was already on her second pretzel. "I left my copy in my locker, which is basically a revolution against homework."

"That's not what revolution means."

"It is now." Inaaya flicked a pretzel salt crystal at her.

Paisley flipped through the photocopied pages, which had been circulating around the back of the bus all afternoon, and found the scene where the soldier visits the White family. "Okay, here. Sergeant-Major Morris tells them the paw grants three wishes, but he says the results are terrible. Then he actually throws the thing into the fire." She looked up. "He throws it in. On purpose. Into the flames."

Prince leaned over the seat from behind them, because Prince leaned over the seat during every bus ride, it was practically his job. "So wait, it's like the story warned them before anything bad happened? The guy straight up says wishes go wrong, then he tries to burn the paw, and they still keep it?"

"Mr. White fishes it out of the fire," Paisley said, running her finger down the page. "Right here. He rescues it."

"Then he deserves whatever monkey business he gets," Prince said, and Inaaya snorted so hard a pretzel went down the wrong pipe.

Paisley stared at the paragraph. Something was clicking, the way a lock clicks, or maybe the way a vending machine finally accepts your coin after three tries. "So this is foreshadowing, right? The warning tells us what's coming. And the fire is... the fire is a symbol? Morris throwing it in means he wants to destroy temptation, and the family pulling it out means they can't resist?" She scribbled in her notebook: warning + fire = doomed family, and underlined "doomed" twice.

"Prove it," said Inaaya, in the voice of a lawyer on a TV show. "How do you know the fire means anything? Maybe he was just cold."

Paisley tested the idea the only way she could on a school bus. "If the fire meant nothing, the writer wouldn't bother making Morris say the wishes are terrible first. You'd just have a guy tossing junk in a fireplace. But the warning plus the fire plus the rescue, that's a pattern. Ms. Cheung said today that when details pile up like that, they're pointing at something." She tapped her pen against her knee. "It's like an anonymous note. Nobody signs it, but if you get three of them, you believe the message."

Prince groaned. "That's going to be your whole presentation, isn't it? Monkey paw plus fire equals doom, the end."

"No, the end is Mr. White standing there holding a crispy paw he pulled out of a fire after being told it ruins lives." Paisley flipped to the last page, where the knocking begins, and her eyes went wide. "Oh. Oh, Prince, they made the first wish on money, and the very next day there's compensation money at the door. The story warned everyone, and they wished anyway."

The bus shuddered to a stop at Maple Court, and Inaaya gathered her pretzel bag. "Tomorrow when you present, do the knocking voice," she said, backing down the aisle. "Knock knock knock, real slow."

Paisley grinned and rapped three times on the window as the bus pulled away.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
story:
The air in the sanctuary smelled like old wood and candle wax, and Matteo's throat felt dry every time he opened his prayer book. In nine days he would stand at the reading table and chant his bar mitzvah portion from the Torah scroll, and so far he could only get through it with his mother's voice mouthing the words from the second row. His friend Edmund had already learned his whole portion, which made it worse.

Mr. Carvalho, the caretaker who unlocked the ark each Sunday, unrolled the scroll to the right place and weighted the corners. "Practice standing up," he said. "Your voice is different on your feet." Matteo stood, and at first it was true in a strange way, like a turbine spinning faster because more water hit it: the words accelerated, and he lost his place in the middle of a verse. His finger drifted toward the parchment to hold his spot.

Mr. Carvalho cleared his throat, not unkindly, and held out a slim silver pointer shaped like a hand with one long finger. "Use the yad," he said. "It means hand." Matteo took it. The metal was cool, and when he set the fingertip of the pointer just under the line he was chanting, the words stopped running away from him. He followed each letter, and the letters stayed.

Afterward, on the synagogue steps, Matteo turned the yad over in his pocket, where Mr. Carvalho had let him keep it for the week. He had an idea, and he wanted to test it. He had lost his place because his eyes jumped; so maybe the problem was not his memory at all, maybe his memory was fine and his eyes were the traitors. That night he covered the line below the one he was reading with a strip of card, and recited the whole portion twice without a single stumble. He covered the line above too, and the third time he closed his eyes and the words came out whole, distinct and steady, like water finding its channel.

On the morning of the ceremony, his mother's hands shook more than his did. Edmund sat in the second row and gave him a small nod, and Matteo's father leaned forward with the video camera. The scroll was open, the yad was in his hand, and his voice did not accelerate or stall. He followed the letters with the silver finger, one line, then the next, all the way to the end of the portion.

When he stepped back, Mr. Carvalho was beaming, and Matteo held out the pointer to return it. Mr. Carvalho shook his head. "Keep it until Sunday," he said. "I have a bar mitzvah student coming who bites his nails, and I want him to see what steady hands look like." Matteo closed his fingers around the little silver hand and grinned. "Send him to me," he said. "I'll teach him the card trick."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Peyton stood at the edge of the school gymnasium with her hands stuffed in her pockets, feeling the glow stick bracelet Ms. Ramos had handed her at the door. The whole gym had been decorated for the dance with streamers and a fog machine, but the lights were so low that everything looked like shadows wearing party hats. Somewhere across the floor, Katrina and Octavia were already dancing, their bracelets throwing green light onto the bleachers.

"Yours didn't turn on," Octavia said, appearing beside her with a frown. "Mine's lit and yours isn't. Maybe yours is dead."

Peyton turned the bracelet over in her fingers. It felt the same as Octavia's, smooth and slightly stiff. Then she remembered something she had read in the science kit her aunt gave her, the one she studied instead of practicing dance moves. The light didn't come from a battery or a switch. It came from bending. When you bent the stick, you broke a thin glass vial of hydrogen peroxide hidden inside it, and that let the peroxide mix with other chemicals and a dye, and that reaction made the light. The word for it popped into her head the way a password does.

"You have to snap it," she said. "Watch."

She bent the bracelet slowly. She felt a tiny crunch under the plastic, so small she almost missed it, like stepping on a grain of sand. Then the green bloomed along the tube from the middle outward, chasing the darkness.

Katrina leaned in, squinting at it. "Where's the light even coming from?"

"Breaking the glass inside," Peyton said. "It's called chemiluminescence."

"That's the longest word anybody has said at this dance," Katrina said, and Octavia laughed.

Peyton looked around the gym. Half the kids near the door were holding dark bracelets, holding them up to their ears and shaking them, waiting for light that would never come on its own. A boy near the water fountain had already dropped his in the trash. Peyton fished it out, wiped it on her sleeve, and bent it until it crackled. It flared yellow.

She spent the next ten minutes salvaging dead bracelets from the trash can and the bleachers and the corner by the scoreboard, snapping each one and handing the glow back to confused sixth graders. Soon the whole doorway looked like a constellation. Ms. Ramos watched from the punch table with her eyebrows raised.

"Half of these were about to be thrown away," Peyton said.

"That was quick thinking," Ms. Ramos said. "There's a science fair in the spring, you know. The winners get a scholarship for summer camp." She tapped her temple. "Keep that fertile imagination going and you might be the one on stage."

Peyton had come to the dance convinced the whole night would be a disaster, that she would stand at the edge until it was over. Now a crowd of kids followed her toward the floor, each one carrying a light she had woken up. Katrina grabbed her wrist, the yellow one still glowing in Peyton's hand.

"Come on, science girl," Katrina said. "Show us what else glows."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.
story:
Julia spread the supplies across the science fair table and felt her stomach drop. Two stacks of litmus paper strips had tumbled out of the box and scattered together, and now she could not tell which strip was which colour to begin with, because every single one looked faintly purple under the gymnasium lights. Agathe leaned over her shoulder and groaned.

"My whole booth depends on this," Agathe said. "The judges are coming at eleven, and I want that blue ribbon more than anything. We're supposed to test liquids and say if each one is an acid or a base, and half of our strips are mixed up." She picked one up, sniffed it, and put it down. "It just smells like paper."

Julia turned the strips over in her fingers. They were dry and thin, like the paper strips her mother used to test the pool water in summer. She wondered whether the colour hiding in them only woke up when something touched it. Could she use a liquid she already knew about, one with an answer she was sure of, and watch what the strip did? Then she could work out the rule, like solving for a hidden number.

"Get me the vinegar and the baking soda mix from our supply bin," Julia said. Agathe grabbed two small cups, and their friend Zackery slid a folded note across the table before hurrying back to his own booth. Julia opened it. "Ask the teacher? That's what I'd do," it read, in Zackery's cramped handwriting. She smiled, folded the note, and tucked it in her pocket, then dipped one purple-ish strip into the vinegar. The strip turned red at once, clean and bright as a candy wrapper. She dipped another strip into the baking soda mix, and that one turned blue, like the sky switching on. So the paper answered differently depending on the liquid.

"Okay," Julia said slowly, watching the strips dry. "Blue litmus paper turns red when you dip it in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when you dip it in a base." She paraphrased it again in her head, shorter this time: acid flips blue to red, base flips red to blue. That meant she could sort the whole pile. She dipped each mystery strip into plain water first, where nothing changed, then into vinegar. The strips that turned red had started as blue, and the ones that stayed pale had started as red. She sorted them into two labelled piles, and Agathe wrote pH numbers from the scale across the top of the poster, pairing each liquid with its strip result.

Mr. Asante paused at their booth on his rounds and watched Julia demonstrate the vinegar test twice, just to be sure. "That's an influential experiment for a sixth grader," he said. "Simple, and it proves something you can't see." Agathe grinned and pinned up a sign that read, in Zackery's words, "our booth runs like a litmus test: quick as a simile, twice as true." Julia laughed and held the red strip up to the light, turning it slowly, still red, still steady.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The number of protons decides which element an atom is: any atom with eight protons is oxygen, and an atom with seven protons is nitrogen.
story:
Megan spread her science notes across the kitchen table and glared at the photocopied periodic table like it had insulted her. Each box held a name, a symbol, and a small whole number in the corner, and tomorrow Mr. Njoroge was giving a quiz on what those numbers meant. She had been absent the day he taught it, because two weeks ago she had chosen to skip review and help her mom carry boxes to the car instead. Helping had felt right at the time. Now she wondered if that had been a permanent mistake.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Rayna: "You missed the wild part of class. Njoroge asked what happens if an oxygen atom somehow lost a proton. Nobody got it. He said it wouldn't be oxygen anymore. It would be nitrogen. SEVEN protons, whole different element. Wild, right?" Megan read the message three times. An atom losing one proton and becoming a different thing sounded like a magic trick, except it was chemistry.

She looked at the oxygen box. Number eight, symbol O. Then nitrogen, right beside it, number seven. So the number in the corner had to be the count of protons, and the count of protons decided what the element was. That was the hidden rule underneath all these boxes. She wanted to see if it held everywhere, so she cut eleven small paper squares, wrote a number on each from one to eleven, and laid them in a row above the table like a homemade number line. Above the eight she placed a marker labeled O. Above the seven she placed N. Then she checked the chart for every other number: one was H, two He, six C, eleven Na. The pattern held across the whole row.

"So it's not the name that makes it what it is," she said out loud to the empty kitchen. "It's the number." An atom with eight protons was oxygen no matter what you called it. An atom with seven was nitrogen. One proton, that was the whole difference between the air she was breathing and the stuff that made up water.

She thought about the boxes in the car two weeks ago, and about her grandmother's old compost bin in the yard, where leaves and peels slowly decomposed into dark soil. Nothing there changed into something else entirely; it just broke down. But an atom changing its proton count was different, a switch, not a fading. She tried to think of a ratio to describe it, like eight to seven, but that didn't quite capture it either. Some things were switches, not fractions.

A knock came at the back door. Josue stood there with his own crumpled periodic table. "Quiz tomorrow," he said. "I don't get any of it. Did you figure out the numbers?"

"Sit down," Megan said, and slid the row of paper squares toward him. "Guess which one is oxygen."

He pointed at the square marked eleven. She grinned and moved his finger back to the eight.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
story:
Emilia had never been away from home for more than two nights, and now she was signed up for three weeks at Camp Winnow, which her mother kept calling "a very prestigious place." On the first morning Emilia stood in the dining hall line holding a tray, staring at the wooden sign above the door. It read American Camp Association, Accredited. Below it, in smaller letters, was a faded line: Founded 1910 as the Camp Directors Association of America.

"What's that mean?" she asked the boy ahead of her, whose name tag said Fynn.

"Beats me," he said. "I think they're the people who enforce the rules. Like camp police."

Emilia filed that away. Camp police. Rules that somebody, somewhere, had agreed on together. That sounded like the kind of thing you could look up, and she wanted to look it up, because Ms. Rowe, the dining hall director, had just announced a rule that seemed aimed straight at her: nobody got seconds on pancakes until every table had been served first.

By day three, Emilia had a theory. Ms. Rowe's rule wasn't real, she decided. It was invented on the spot to slow down table six, where Emilia sat with Fynn and Demi and where the pancakes always ran out first. Her evidence was a pattern: table six got served last every single meal, no matter when they arrived. That wasn't a rule working fairly. That was a rule being used.

"We test it," she told Demi at lunch, twisting the polymer beads on her bracelet, a camp craft she'd finished that morning. "Tomorrow we come early, sit at table two, and see if we get served first."

They came early. They sat at table two. Ms. Rowe walked past table six, past table four, and set the first platter of pancakes down in front of Emilia.

"See?" Emilia whispered. "It's the table, not the rule."

Then Ms. Rowe kept standing there. "Table six tells me you three switched," she said. "That's fine. But the early-tables-first rule applies to where you sat all week, not where you sit today. Back of the line for seconds."

Demi cracked up. Fynn slid his fork toward the platter and said, "Fair is fair. Hand me three."

After breakfast, Emilia found the old camp handbook in the craft shed, a thin booklet from decades back. Inside the cover someone had glued the original charter page, dated 1910. The Camp Directors Association of America, it said, had been formed to set common standards for organized camps. Common standards. Not invented ones. Not rules aimed at table six. Rules that every camp everywhere had agreed to follow, written down before her mother was born.

Emilia carried the booklet to the dining hall and set it on the counter in front of Ms. Rowe.

"Table six," Ms. Rowe said, pointing with her spatula at the day's seating chart, where Emilia's name had been moved to the very last table, next to the door and the trash bins.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
Nathaniel slid his phone across the dinner table, screen up, and waited. "Look at this dress and tell me what color it is."

His father squinted at it first. "White and gold. Obviously."

"Mom?"

His mother leaned over, still holding the serving spoon. "Blue and black." She set the spoon down and looked at his father like he was joking. "It's blue and black, right there."

"That dress is white," his father said, "with gold bands."

Nathaniel had found the photo at school, when Blakely and Salman had nearly come to blows over it in the cafeteria. Salman saw white and gold; Blakely saw blue and black; and Nathaniel, standing between them, had seen something so strange he couldn't stop thinking about it. Now the same fight had followed him home. He turned the phone around and looked again himself. Blue and black, plain as anything.

"Everybody stop," he said, and put the phone flat in the middle of the table, next to the mashed potatoes. "We're all looking at the exact same picture, right? Same screen, same light in the room."

His mother nodded slowly. His father crossed his arms, which meant he was getting interested despite himself.

"Okay," Nathaniel said. "So if we see different colors, something's going on that we can't see. Something behind it." He didn't know what yet, but he had a plan. He carried the phone to the window, where the last gray daylight came through, and held it up. "Dad, look from here." His father came over, leaned in, and his face changed.

"Huh," his father said. "Still white and gold. But now I almost see how you'd get blue out of it."

Nathaniel's mother waved them back. "Let me try the window." She looked, then laughed once, short and surprised. "From here it's even more blue. Like the sky trying to coordinate with the curtains."

They moved around the kitchen like scientists, holding the phone under the bright range hood, then in the dim hallway, then back at the table. Nobody switched all the way over, but everybody wobbled. His father admitted the blue "showed up sometimes." His mother said the gold "peeked through at certain angles." The photo was doing something strange to all of them, the same thing it had done to Blakely and Salman, and Nathaniel wrote down who saw what, where, under which light, trying to find the pattern.

That night he texted Salman and Blakely the question his father had finally asked out loud: "But what color is it really?" Salman answered fast with a link. Blakely answered faster, in all caps: "IT WAS ON THE NEWS. THE REAL DRESS IS BLUE AND BLACK. THEY SHOWED IT."

Nathaniel stared at the message. So his mother had been right, and Salman and his father had been wrong, but not because their eyes were broken. Two people could look at the same exact thing and honestly see two different worlds, and the thing itself could still have one true answer underneath it. He sat with that for a while, the phone warm in his hand.

The next morning he printed the photo and brought it to Ms. Lombardi's room before the bell. He laid it on her desk without any explanation and watched her push her glasses up to look.

"Blue and black," she said.

"Half the eighth grade says white and gold," Nathaniel said, and slid a second copy across the desk toward her, "so I figured you should get the evidence too."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Max had taped a giant poster of the soccer schedule to the back of the garden shed, and every Saturday he marched across the backyard with a marker to record the results. A green dot for a win, a red dot for a loss. So far the poster looked like a lopsided Christmas tree: six red dots in a row on the top half, then three green dots stacked underneath, and tomorrow was game number ten.

"What's the chart for?" Billie asked, dropping onto the stable old bench beside the shed, the one that never wobbled no matter how they flopped onto it. Billie had come over with cleats dangling from one hand and a granola bar already half eaten.

"Watch this," Max said. He tapped the red dots. "Every game away, we lose. Every game at our own field, we win." He tapped the green dots. "It's not luck. Something's going on, and I want to figure out what before tomorrow, because tomorrow is at home."

Ophelia arrived just in time to hear that, and she frowned at the poster like it was a puzzle with a piece missing. "Maybe we're just better when nobody's yelling at us," she said. "Away crowds are loud."

"Or maybe it's the field," Max said. "Our grass is different. Our goals are the ones we practice on." He had a theory, and theories needed testing. "Here's my test. Tomorrow, when we play at home, I'm going to keep count of how many passes we complete versus how many we completed last week at Riverside. If it's the field, the numbers should jump."

Saturday came, and the backyard was the meeting spot before the game because Max's house was closest to the park. Mr. Wu, the neighbour whose tomato plants bordered the fence, waved them over and handed out orange slices from a bowl. "Big match today?" he asked.

"We're trying to conquer our away-game curse," Max told him. "But today's home, so we should win."

Mr. Wu smiled. "You know, across lots of sports, home teams win more than half their games on average. They call it home advantage."

Max stared at him. It wasn't just his team. It was a thing that happened everywhere, in sport after sport, big enough that somebody had given it a name. On the field an hour later, he counted passes while he played: thirty-one completed, nine more than at Riverside. They beat their toughest adversary, the undefeated Maplewood team, four to two, and the home crowd roared so loudly Max felt it in his ribs.

That evening he added a fourth green dot to the poster, then wrote HOME in careful capitals beside it. He had one more test left, and he was already planning it: next away game, he would count the crowd noise and the passes both, side by side, all game long. Billie jogged over with the marker. "Add the score," Billie said. "Four to two. In giant letters."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Dylan had the laptop open on the coffee table, but the argument had taken over the whole living room. "Marcus Bell is the best hitter on the team and nobody talks about him," Imran said, jabbing a finger at the screen where Bell's stats glowed. "He's only batting .260. That's middle of the pack," Isis said from the couch, where she was gluing a new propeller onto the model plane she'd been building all week. "Middle of the pack," Imran repeated, disgusted. "The rankings are biased against him. I'm telling you."

Dylan scrolled down the page while they argued. He liked numbers better than arguments, because numbers could be checked. Bell had 412 at-bats and 107 hits, and Dylan did the division in his notebook just to be sure it came out to about .260. It did. But a column farther right caught his eye. Walks: 94. Ninety-four times Bell had walked up to the plate, waited out the pitcher, and gotten on base without swinging. Dylan checked the next thing carefully, because it seemed strange. Those 94 walks were not included anywhere in the 412 at-bats. "Hey," he said. "Look at this. Walks don't count as at-bats at all."

Isis set down her propeller and came over. "What do you mean, don't count?" "I mean the batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks aren't at-bats," Dylan said, tapping the two columns. "So the average gives Bell no credit for all those walks. It's like they never happened." Imran leaned in so fast he knocked a pillow off the couch. "Ninety-four times. That's ninety-four times he got on base and the number just ignores him."

Dylan decided to test it. He picked another player, the one ranked just above Bell, and laid the two stat lines side by side in his notebook. The other player had more hits and a slightly better average, but only 31 walks. When Dylan counted up every time each player had actually reached base, Bell was ahead by a mile. It wasn't that the ranking was lying exactly, he thought, chewing his pencil. It was that one number had to squeeze a whole season into itself, and things fell out of the squeeze. A season of hundreds of pitches and swings and patient waits, pressed into a single decimal that only knew about some of it.

"There should be a number that counts getting on base, period," Imran said. "Hits, walks, everything." "Somebody probably invented one already," Isis said. "People invent numbers all the time. Like Dad inventing new ways to renovate the basement every summer and never finishing." She went back to her plane, spun the propeller once to test it, and frowned at the wobble.

They searched and found it: on-base percentage, sitting in the next column over, counting walks just the way Imran wanted. Bell ranked third on the team in it. Imran stood up with both fists raised like his team had just won in extra innings. "Third. THIRD. I'm texting my dad." Dylan copied the two columns into his notebook one more time, slowly, so he would remember which number told which story.

Isis held the plane above her head and let it fly across the living room. The propeller caught the light from the window as it circled, wobbled, and landed on the couch. "So," she said, "how long before they invent a stat for most improved model airplane?"

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel, with its two leads touching either end of the component being tested.
story:
Everly's project board said "The Secret Life of Wire" in letters she'd repainted twice, and next to it Katelynn's board said "Owls: Nocturnal Ninjas of the Sky," complete with a plastic owl wearing a tiny headband. The gym smelled like hot glue and nervousness. Everly had one hour to show the judges that a plain length of nichrome wire had a hidden property called resistance, and she was going to extract it from nothing but numbers.

The plan was simple. She would push current through the wire with a battery pack, measure the voltage across it, measure the current through it, and divide. Voltage divided by current equals resistance, Ohm's law, done. But when she clipped her circuit together, the numbers went strange. The current reading made sense. The voltage reading was nearly zero, as if the wire had no resistance at all, which would make her whole project a very short story.

"Maybe your wire's just lazy," Katelynn said, patting her plastic owl. "Mine works night shifts."

"Wire can't be lazy," Everly said, though she glared at it anyway. Taya leaned over the table, chewing a pretzel.

"Where'd you put the voltmeter?" Taya asked.

Everly pointed. She had clipped both voltmeter leads into the same spot on one end of the wire, side by side, like two people standing in the same doorway. Taya snorted so hard a pretzel crumb hit the owl.

"Both ends," Everly said slowly, and it was like a light coming on in a room she hadn't known was dark. "A voltmeter measures voltage, so its leads have to touch either end of the thing. One on each end. Across it." She moved one lead to the far end of the wire, and the two leads now bridged the whole component, in parallel with it, touching both ends at once. The needle jumped. Two point four volts.

"Now divide," Taya said, mouth full.

"Zero point three amps," Everly read off the ammeter. She scribbled on the back of her hand, because of course her notebook was under the owl. "Two point four divided by zero point three is eight. Eight ohms." She looked at the plain gray wire with new respect. It had been hiding that number the whole time, and all she'd had to do was ask it from both ends.

A shadow fell across her board. Ms. Murphy, clipboard in hand, was reading her title with one eyebrow up.

"So," Ms. Murphy said. "Show me the mechanism."

Everly picked up the leads, one in each hand, and touched them to opposite ends of the wire. "Watch the needle," she said.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Laurence set her fork down and slid the dress catalog across the table. "I want this one," she said. "The white one with the sash."

Her mother kept cutting her chicken. Her grandmother put down her teacup so fast it clicked against the saucer.

"Not white," Grandmother said.

"Why not? It's a wedding." Laurence turned the page toward her. "Cousin Sophie's getting married in June. I already saved the money from shoveling Mr. Cardinal's walk all winter. This is how I acquire it. Earned money, my choice."

"Choose another color," Grandmother said. "Any color. Blue. Pink. Not white."

Laurence looked at her mother, who shrugged in a way that meant the verdict was already in and it wasn't going to be appealed.

"That's not fair," Laurence said. "Everyone wears white to weddings."

"Not everyone," said Grandmother, and she went back to her rice.

Laurence sat there chewing on it, the way she chewed on math problems that wouldn't break open. Fair was one thing. Not explaining was another. After dinner she carried the photo album to the table, the old one from the shelf under the window, and opened it to the picture from her great-uncle's funeral three years ago. Everyone in dark clothes. Except her grandmother, in white. Plain white, head to toe. She flipped to Grandmother's own wedding photos from Hong Kong. Red dress. Gold trim. No white anywhere.

She carried the album back to the living room, where Grandmother was folding laundry.

"Why were you wearing white at the funeral?" Laurence asked. "You always tell me white is for brides."

"In our tradition, white is what we wear for mourning at funerals," Grandmother said. She smoothed a towel flat. "Here, the bride wears white and everyone thinks it is beautiful. Different eyes, different meaning. Same color."

Laurence looked at the two pictures side by side, then at her catalog page. Two weddings. Two dresses. One color that meant two opposite things, and nobody had thought to tell her.

"So if I wore the white dress to Sophie's wedding," she said slowly, "it would be fine for the groom's family, because they're not Chinese. But when we take photos with your side..."

Grandmother didn't say anything. She just went on folding, but her shoulders had come down from around her ears.

The next evening Laurence came to the dinner table with the catalog again, the white page folded behind the blue one. "The blue dress," she said. "And one question."

Grandmother raised an eyebrow.

"You still have the red silk scarf from your wedding photos. Could I wear that?"

Grandmother got up without a word and went to the tall dresser in the hall. She came back with something wrapped in tissue paper and set it beside Laurence's plate.

"Try it," she said. "See if it suits you."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Daniel spread his paper airplane notes across the library table and discovered he had two experiments instead of one. On Monday he had flown a dart plane and a glider, but the dart was folded from heavy cardstock and the glider from thin printer paper, so he could not tell whether wing shape or paper weight had made the difference. The science fair was in nine days, and his data sheet was a mess.

Baylee slid into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "Still on the airplanes?"

"Look at this," Daniel said, turning the sheet toward her. "The glider flew farther, but it was also lighter. Two things changed at once."

Baylee tapped the page. "So change one thing on purpose and measure the other thing." She pulled a book from her stack and flipped to a page she had obviously already read. "The one you change on purpose is called the independent variable."

Daniel copied the phrase onto a fresh index card. He would keep the paper weight exactly the same for every plane, heavy cardstock only, and change nothing but the wing shape. Then he could measure flight distance and know the shape was what made the difference. He logged into the library computer and searched the catalog database for books on paper airplane design, found two on the third floor, and went up the stairs two at a time.

Benson was already in the aviation aisle, holding a book called The Gliding Handbook. When Daniel explained his plan, Benson frowned. "You should also throw from different heights. More height, more distance, everyone knows that."

"That would be another thing changing," Daniel said. "I'd be gullible to believe the wing shape worked when maybe the height did it." They argued quietly until Ms. Dang, the librarian, appeared at the end of the shelf and asked them to take it to the study room. Inside, Daniel drew a diagram: one arrow labeled "what I change," one labeled "what I measure," and a line through everything else.

That evening he found a message from Baylee on his screen. "Checked the weather for Saturday. Winds are supposed to coincide with the time we planned to fly outside. If wind pushes the planes, that's another thing changing. Gym at school instead? My dad can get us in at ten."

Daniel read it twice, then typed back one word and grabbed his cardstock. "Gym."

He was already folding the first plane when his mom called him to dinner, and he set it on the windowsill, wings spread, waiting for morning.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
story:
The lemonade stand had earned Daniel thirty-seven dollars in two weeks, and at that rate the new bike would arrive sometime around his sixteenth birthday. He had taped a graph to the front of the stand, two lines crawling across it in different colors, and he stared at it between customers while the pitcher sweated in the shade.

"You're doing math at a lemonade stand," Maggie said, counting quarters into the cash box. "That's grim, even for you."

"It's my budget," Daniel said. "Thirty-seven dollars, every two weeks, into the bank. Mr. Han at the credit union said I could pick plain simple interest or compound interest, and I'm trying to see which one wins." He tapped the red line, straight as a ruler across the page. "Simple interest adds the same amount every year. This one just goes up like a ramp."

Maggie squinted at the blue line, which bent gently upward, like a fishing rod with something heavy on the hook. "So the blue one's broken?"

"That's what I thought yesterday." He flipped to his second sheet, where he had plotted the balance year by year for five years. The red line climbed evenly, the same step each time. The blue line's steps got taller. "It's not broken. Compound interest gains more each year than the year before. So it curves. It starts almost on top of the red one, and then they pull apart." He traced the widening gap with his finger. "By year five the blue one's way up here."

A woman bought two cups and said the lemonade was exceptional, which made Maggie stand a little straighter. When she'd gone, Maggie pulled a sock full of bills from her backpack and set it on the counter without looking at him. "That's my jar money. Sixty-two dollars. It was for concert tickets."

Daniel didn't touch it. "You don't have to."

"The tickets are sold out anyway," Maggie said, in a voice that suggested they weren't, and that she had decided something anyway. She turned the sock over, and the bills slid out onto the counter, soft and creased. "Put it in the curvy one."

"The compound one," Daniel said. "Yeah." He stacked the bills, wrote sixty-two dollars under the day's total, and drew a small blue dot on the graph, one step higher than where the line had been that morning. Then he taped the sock flat against the inside wall of the stand, right beside the graph, so they could both watch the gap grow.

"Pitcher's empty," Maggie said, and picked it up. "We'd better squeeze some more if we're going to beat the rain." The sky to the west had gone the color of wet slate, and the weather app was flashing its little precipitation icon, so Daniel grabbed the bag of lemons from the cooler and got to work.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
Piper marched up to the vegetable stall at the farmers' market with five dollars and a plan: she was going to make pasta sauce from scratch, better than the stuff from a jar. Mr. MacLeod, who ran the stall and apparently also ran a Saturday cooking table beside it, raised an eyebrow at her empty hands.

"No knife?" he said. "Then you can borrow mine, as long as you learn the claw grip first. Curl your fingertips under, like a cat's paw, and let your knuckles guide the blade. The knife can nick a nail, but it can't get at your fingertips, because they're tucked away."

Piper curled her fingers and sawed at an onion, which fought back by making her eyes stream so badly that Ayla, watching from a crate of pumpkins, laughed until she wheezed. "You look like you watched a sad movie about onions," Ayla said. "It's the onion trying to irritate your eyes, and winning." Piper kept going, and by the third onion her cuts were almost even, and her fingers were still attached, which she counted as a victory.

She set a portable burner on the table and poured in oil. Mr. MacLeod was busy weighing tomatoes for a frail old woman who moved slowly down the row of baskets, so Piper dumped the onion and the garlic into the pan together, cranked the heat to high because high meant faster, and went to fetch the tomatoes. When she came back, the garlic was dark brown and the whole pan smelled sharp in a bad way. She stirred it into the sauce anyway and handed Ayla a spoon.
