Ayla's face folded in on itself. "It's bitter," she said. "Like, actually bitter. What did you do?"

Piper stared at the pan. The onion looked fine, golden and soft. The garlic was the burnt part. She thought about the timing: everything had gone in at once, but only one thing had burned. Maybe they weren't the same. She scraped the sauce into the compost bucket, which hurt, and turned to Mr. MacLeod. "If I do it again," she said, "should the garlic go in after the onion's soft?"

"Now you're cooking," he said, and handed her another clove.

The second batch, she took at leisure, letting the onions soften slowly, breathing in the sweet smell instead of sprinting through it. Only when they went limp and glassy did she slide the chopped garlic in, stir for half a minute, and pour in the crushed tomatoes. The sauce burbled. Sally from her science class wandered over, sniffed, and stole the stirring spoon before anyone could stop her.

"Okay, that one's good," Sally said, going back for seconds. "That one's really good."

Piper ladled sauce over a bowl of pasta Mr. MacLeod produced from somewhere, and Ayla held up her spoon like a sword. "Third batch," she said, "you get to name it."

"Claw Grip Red," Piper said, and took the first bite.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Ryder spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at his graph like it had betrayed him. Tomorrow was the science fair, and his project, which plant seeds sprout fastest when you soak them first, had taken eleven days of careful work. He had timed, watered, and measured. But when Johanna came over to check the poster, she had squinted at his chart and said, "Wait. Why is soaking time going up and down the side?"

Now, alone with the lamp on and his mom humming in the next room, Ryder looked again. Along the horizontal axis he had written "number of sprouts." Up the vertical side he had written "soaking time in hours." It looked fine at a glance. It looked fine for eleven days, in fact. But something about it bothered him, the way a tiny fracture in a cup bothers you only after you spot it.

He called Johanna, because she was the one who noticed things. "Bring your brother's math binder," he said when she arrived with Maximilian trailing behind her, carrying the binder like it might intimidate him. Maximilian flipped through pages of homework until he found a scatter plot from last autumn. On that one, time sat along the bottom. On every graph in the binder, along every bottom edge, sat the thing the experimenter had chosen: the hours studied, the days measured, the temperatures set.

"So the thing I control goes on the bottom," Ryder said slowly, "horizontal, the x-axis. And the thing that happens because of it goes up the side, vertical, the y-axis." Johanna nodded. "You changed the soaking time. The sprouts happened because of it." Ryder groaned. His graph had them swapped. Anyone who knew graphs would look at his poster and think he had changed the number of sprouts to see what soaking time came out, which made no sense at all.

He started over with a fresh sheet, and Maximilian slid the pencil sharpener across the table without being asked. Johanna read numbers aloud from his notebook while Ryder plotted each point: zero hours, four hours, eight hours, twelve. As the dots took shape, the pattern rose and rose, then dipped, because after twelve hours of soaking the seeds actually sprouted more slowly. "A twist," Johanna said, tapping the dip. "You found that more isn't always better."

The doorbell rang, and Mr. O'Brien from next door stood there holding a plate of cookies, because he had heard about the fair through the fence. He had once judged a county fair, and his weathered face went turbulent with worry when Ryder mentioned tornado posters, until Ryder clarified it was a seed project, and the worry broke into a grin. Mr. O'Brien stayed for cocoa while Ryder practiced his speech, and when Ryder said "soaking time on the x-axis, sprouts on the y-axis," the old man clapped once, sharp and pleased.

Ryder had almost decided to skip the fair that morning, convinced his mistake had ruined everything. Now he pinned the redone graph to the poster, stepped back, and read the rising line and its honest little dip out loud one more time. Johanna held the door. "Bring the good pencil," Ryder said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
The box sat on the kitchen table between Carson's elbows, and he had already read every word on it twice. His grandfather leaned over from his chair, tapping the slim phone through the cardboard. "You know the phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about one point one kilograms?" he said. "Two and a half pounds. Like carrying a brick with a battery strapped to it." Carson's mother laughed, and Carson slid the box closer to himself, because the moment felt like it could still be taken back.

"Before you open it," she said, "we need to talk about the rules that will govern it. Screen time limits. No phone at dinner. Charger stays in the kitchen overnight." Carson nodded along, but inside he was doing the math. His mother worked early shifts. She could not actually see whether he used the phone at midnight, which meant the rules only held if he held them, which meant the whole arrangement depended on something invisible. That bothered him more than any single rule did.

He opened the box at the table, set the phone on the kitchen scale his grandfather used for bread dough, and watched the numbers settle: 174 grams. He did the subtraction in his head, twice, because it seemed absurd. "The first one was more than six times heavier than this," he said. His grandfather nodded, already reaching for his coffee. "Progress," he said, and did not explain further, which was his way.

That night Carson lay awake thinking about the invisible part again. If nobody could see what he did with the phone, maybe the phone itself could see, and maybe he could test that. At breakfast he told his plan to Leonardo, who came by before school with his own phone face-down on the table like contraband. "I think the battery drain is proportional to how much I actually use it," Carson said. "So tonight I'm charging to one hundred percent, then leaving it alone for exactly one hour, then one hour of just videos. If the numbers drop the same both hours, the drain is random and my test is useless. If they're different, I've got a record of my own behavior that nobody had to watch."

Leonardo squinted at him. "You're making your phone the antagonist of your own week." "It's not the antagonist," Carson said. "I am, if I cheat. The phone's just the witness."

The first test ran that evening. One hour untouched, battery at 100 percent, and the number didn't move at all, not even one percent, which he wrote in his notebook. Then an hour of videos, and the screen lit up with his mother's text before he could record the second number: How's the new phone treating you?

He typed back, Perfect, and sent her the photo of the kitchen scale with 174 grams on it, then the notebook page with his first result. Three dots appeared. Then: Leftover pizza in the fridge if you want it after your next test. He set the phone down, face-up this time, and started the video hour.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: To clear a fraction from an equation, multiply both sides by its denominator: if x divided by 3 equals 5, multiplying both sides by 3 gives x = 15.
story:
The community centre smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee, and the vending machine in the corner hummed a single low note that never stopped. Nicolas sat at the folding table by the window, three crumpled dollar bills and two quarters in front of him, staring at a worksheet that Ms. Wu had handed out at the start of the homework club. Across the top it said "Linear Equations, One Variable," and the first problem read: x divided by 3 equals 5. He had been on it for ten minutes.

Lev dropped into the chair beside him and slid a receipt across the table. "The vending machine ate my money. I put in five dollars for the pizza rolls and nothing came out." He jiggled the coin return, then gave up and sat back down. Mavrik, on Nicolas's other side, was already shaking the machine by its corners, which the coach had told him twice this month was reckless, since the last boy who did it had cracked a shelf.

Nicolas looked from the worksheet to the receipt and back. Something about the number five was bothering him, so he tried saying the problem out loud in a different way. "Something divided by three is five. Like a bill." Lev frowned. "What bill?" "Any bill," Nicolas said. "Three people, each pays five dollars, and nobody knows the total." He wrote a small 3 beside the fraction and thought about the summer, when he and his cousins had split the cost of a giant slushie and had to work backward from what each of them had paid to figure out what the cup had cost in the first place. His uncle had refused to tell them, and they had puzzled it out on a napkin before the ice even melted.

He picked up his pencil. If each share was five dollars, and there were three shares, then multiplying both sides by 3 gave x equals 15. He did the same thing to each side, the way the worksheet seemed to want, and wrote it down. Fifteen dollars total. Mavrik leaned over. "Do it to the other one." The next problem had a 4 on the bottom, so Nicolas multiplied both sides by 4, and the fraction vanished like a smudge wiped off glass.

"That's it," Ms. Wu said from the doorway, and Nicolas felt his ears go warm. She did not explain anything; she only tapped the paper twice and moved on to the next table.

Later, walking out through the lobby, Lev confided that he had exactly fifteen dollars left in his wallet, saved for the guild gaming tournament on Saturday. They passed the vending machine, and Mavrik gave it one last hopeful thump. The metal rack shivered, and a bag of pizza rolls thumped down into the tray, followed by the machine spitting Lev's five dollars back into the coin return, every coin of it. "Free pizza rolls," Mavrik said, holding the bag up to the light. Lev pulled out the five and looked at Nicolas. "So if we split those three ways," he said, "I owe you each about a dollar sixty-six."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
Georgia had slathered on sunscreen at nine that morning, in the parking lot, while her dad wrestled the cooler and her mom enforced the family rule that nobody touched the sand until every ear and neck was covered. By eleven she and Eva-Rose had dug a trench to the waterline, and by noon they had been swimming three times, toweling off, and swimming again. Now it was almost two, and the backs of Georgia's shoulders had begun to sting in a way she did not like.

"Your face is pink," Eva-Rose said, squinting at her. "Like, actually pink, not just warm-pink."

"It can't be," Georgia said. "I put sunscreen on. This morning. You saw me." She pulled her towel around her shoulders like a cape, which helped and also hid the pink.

They had made a settlement before the trip that they would trade off who chose the activities, and so far it had held: Georgia had picked the trench, Eva-Rose had picked swimming. The problem, Georgia thought as she sat in the shade of the umbrella and stared at the pattern of red on her arms, was that the pattern made no sense. The parts under her swimsuit straps were fine. The parts that had been wet all morning were burned. If the sunscreen worked in the parking lot, why had it stopped working?

She counted backward on her fingers. Nine o'clock, cream on. Twelve thirty, last swim. That was more than two hours. And every single time they came out of the water and toweled off, she had toweled the sunscreen off with the water.

"Eva-Rose," she said slowly. "I think it wears out. The sunscreen. You have to put it on again after two hours, and right away after you swim. Or sweat. That's probably why my shoulders look like this and my strap lines look like nothing."

"So you're saying we have to reapply and get back in the water before the bus comes?" Eva-Rose was already digging in the beach bag. "Because the bus comes at three, and I am not sitting on a hot bus for two hours without swimming."

The bottle was nearly empty. Georgia shook it, got a sad little blob, and offered it to Eva-Rose, who shook her head. "I burn worse than you. You take it."

They reached a settlement on the spot: Georgia would use the last of the bottle, and Eva-Rose would get first pick of the after-school snack for a whole week. Eva-Rose declared this only fair, since the damage to Georgia was, in her words, "clearly not proportional to the snack debt, but close."

Georgia rubbed the cream in circles over her shoulders, wincing, then down her arms, then handed the bottle to Brett, who had been listening from his towel with the expression of a boy who had also been in the water all morning. "My mom said that," he admitted. "This morning. I figured once was enough."

The tide was coming in and the trench was filling, which gave them exactly one thing to do about it. Georgia tied the towel around her waist, ran to the waterline, and shouted over her shoulder, "Half an hour, then we dry off and I get more from the cooler bag, even if I have to use my dad's nose cream."

Eva-Rose was already sprinting past her, kicking spray. "Race you to the sandbar."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Lucy's right knee had been aching for three weeks, so when Brent sent her a link titled "This Bracelet Fixed My Knee in Four Days," she clicked it before her cereal went soggy. The page showed a man named Dan holding up a copper bracelet and grinning. Dan wrote that he had worn it to a wedding, danced all night, and woken up pain free for the first time in two years. Lucy scrolled fast, hunting for the part where Dan explained how it worked. There was no part. There was only Dan, and a button that said Buy Now.

"Mrs. Alvarez wears one," Betty said over video chat that evening. "She swears by it." Betty held her own wrist up to the camera, a thin copper band glinting. "My mom got me this last year when my elbow hurt. And look, my elbow's fine."

Lucy frowned at the screen. "But did you stop playing volleyball that week too? Because I rested my knee last weekend and it felt better by Monday, and I don't own a bracelet."

Betty shrugged. "I mean, I did have a bye week." She twisted the band around her wrist, and for a second she looked less certain.

Lucy opened a new tab and typed Dan's story into the search bar herself. She found a site where a doctor wrote about studies, real ones, where hundreds of people wore either copper bracelets or plain ones that looked identical, and nobody could tell afterward which group had less pain. Lucy read it twice. The people with the fake bracelets reported the same relief. So the copper itself was not doing the work; something else was, and the studies had been built to rule the other explanations out. Dan's story, she realized, could not do that. He got better while wearing the bracelet, but his knee might have healed on its own, or he might have rested it, or he might just have been in a better mood at the wedding.

At school the next morning, Mr. Wong was erasing the whiteboard when Lucy stopped beside his desk. "Is there a word for that," she asked, "when somebody tells one story about themselves and treats it like proof?"

He smiled. "An anecdote."

"Right." Lucy emphasized the word with a nod, like she was filing it somewhere permanent. "Dan's page is an anecdote. The study with the fake bracelets isn't."

"Careful," Mr. Wong said, capping his marker. "Studies can be badly done too. You still have to check." He tapped the board. "Cartilage heals slowly, by the way. Whatever your knee is doing, give it time."

That afternoon Lucy skipped the bracelet link, closed the browser, and pulled her running shoes from the closet only to set them on the top shelf. Then she dug out the old ice pack from the freezer, wrapped it in a dish towel, and propped her knee on a cushion beside the computer. On the screen, Dan's Buy Now button glowed, patient and resilient as ever. Lucy reached over and shut the laptop lid.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Alice peeled a curved slab of onion from the salad bar tray in the museum lab and dropped it onto a slide. Around her, the humid room smelled of vinegar and floor polish. Beside her, Vincenzo already had his sketch page out, half finished.

"Pass the stain," she said. He slid the little dropper bottle across the counter without looking up.

Alice pressed the cover slip down, dropped the slide onto the stage and cranked the lens into place. The eyepiece showed nothing but grey darkness, a solid wall of it. She twisted the focus knob back and forth. Still dark. Vincenzo leaned over.

"You crushed it," he said.

"I didn't touch it."

"Then your onion's broken." He grinned. Lilianne, at the next station, slid her chair over and peered into Alice's eyepiece.

"It's like the tundra in winter at night," she said. "Nothing. Total nothing."

Alice lifted the slide and held it up to the ceiling light. The onion chunk was thick and cloudy, pale greenish white, and it blocked the light like a pebble. She looked across the room at Mr. Yamamoto's demo station, where a paper sign read: onion skin, inner layer only. A shallow dish sat beside it with papery red membrane strips floating in water, the flimsy tissue from between the rings, thin enough that she could see the shadow of her own fingers through it.

She pulled a fresh onion from the tray and cut it open with the safety blade, the way they'd been shown. Inside, between two thick rings, clung a film so fine it folded like tissue paper. She teased a square of it loose with tweezers, laid it flat on a clean slide, added one drop of stain and the cover slip. Her eyes were stinging now, and she wiped them on her sleeve.

This time the eyepiece filled with cells. Rows of neat bricks, each one edged in a darker line, with a small dense spot near the middle. Alice grabbed her pencil.

"That was fast," Vincenzo said, still wrestling with his own dark slide.

"The thick piece was too thick." She tapped the peel of membrane. "Light can't get through it. This inner skin is only one cell thick, so light passes through it."

Lilianne bent to her eyepiece. "Oh. There they are."

Mr. Yamamoto paused behind them, glanced at the slide, and pointed at Alice's blank labels. "Wall, membrane, nucleus. Which line corresponds to which?"

Alice set her pencil down. "The thick outer edge is the wall. The faint line just inside it is the membrane. And this dot," she said, circling the small dense spot twice, "is the nucleus."

She wrote all three labels in her smallest, most careful printing, then slid the slide back under the lens to check them one last time.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Paisley pulled her sneakers off at Vanessa's front door and followed her down the hallway, where Vanessa's dog promptly stepped on one of them. In the den, Theoren sat on the floor surrounded by shoeboxes, holding up a pair of sneakers that looked almost new.

"I don't get it," he said. "These are the second pair this year. My mom is going to lose her mind. And the ironic part is, my jeans from September still fit fine." He recounted the whole saga: new shoes in October, dead by February, while the rest of him, by every other measure, had apparently stayed exactly the same size.

Paisley crouched down and turned one of the old shoes over in her hands. It wasn't worn out; it was genuinely too small. She lined it up against the new pair and saw that his feet had jumped almost a full size in a few months. Meanwhile his jeans, which she had seen him wear just last week, still sat at his ankles like normal. Something was growing out of order, and that interested her more than the shoes themselves.

"Vanessa, do you have a tape measure? And paper?" While Vanessa dug through a kitchen drawer, Paisley laid out her idea. "I think feet and hands grow first, before everything else. Before arms, before legs, before the rest of you. So if Theoren's feet are shooting up and his jeans still fit, his body hasn't caught up yet. Which means it probably will." Theoren groaned. Vanessa said that sounded made up, like something from her brother's gaming guild forums, where people posted theories about everything.

Paisley tested it anyway. She traced Theoren's hand on the paper, then made him stretch his arm out so she could measure from fingertip to shoulder. Then she traced her own hand and measured her own arm, twice, to be sure. Her hands looked big for her arms, the same mismatched pattern as Theoren's feet and jeans. She wrote both sets of numbers down and studied them, chewing the end of the pencil. "Same shape," she said. "Both of us. Big hands, smaller arms. Big feet, same jeans."

Vanessa leaned over the numbers and went quiet for a moment. "Okay," she said slowly, "that's actually weirdly convincing." She held her own hand against the tracing and frowned at it. Theoren stood up, walked to the mirror, and turned sideways, examining his jeans with new suspicion, like they were a bomb with a long fuse.

"So basically," he said, "the shoes were just the first message."

"The very first," Paisley said, and handed him the tape measure. "Hold this. We're measuring your little brother next."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: To remove a tyre, a tyre lever is hooked under the tyre's edge and clipped to a spoke, then a second lever is used a little further along.
story:
The bus shelter smelled of warm asphalt, and the humid air stuck to Juliette's arms as she knelt beside her bike. The front tyre was flat, sagging against the curb like a deflated balloon, and the next bus was forty minutes away. Charles stood over her, shifting his backpack from one shoulder to the other.

"We could still make the four o'clock showing," he said, checking his phone for the third time. "If we lock the bike here and take the bus."

"It's a ten minute ride from my house to school," Juliette said. "If I can't fix a flat, I'll be taking the bus every morning for the rest of the year." She turned the wheel slowly, hunting for the hole. She found it near the valve: a tiny silver thorn, like a splinter of glass, buried in the rubber. She pulled it out and heard the faintest hiss, which meant the tube inside was still leaking. That was the strange part. The puncture was hidden inside a sealed tyre, and she couldn't see it or reach it. She would have to get the tyre off first.

She tried pinching the edge of the tyre and dragging it back over the rim with her thumbs. Her fingers rebelled, slipping off the stiff black rubber every time, and she sat back on her heels. In her repair kit, rolled in an old sock, she found two flat plastic levers, curved like little spoons. There was also a folded paper with hand-drawn diagrams, which her older cousin had scribbled before moving away. Juliette studied it, then looked up at Charles.

"Two levers," she said. "You hook the first one under the edge of the tyre, then clip it to a spoke so it holds itself." She slid the lever's notch under the tyre's edge, leaned on it until a strip of pale inner rubber showed, and hooked the other end around the nearest spoke. The lever stayed there, pinned, doing work her fingers couldn't. She took the second lever and pushed it under the edge a little further along. When she pulled that one back, a whole section of tyre popped free, and she could drag the rest off with her hands.

Charles crouched down beside her, his phone pocketed. "Can I pump it?" he asked. "I've never used one of those." He worked the pump handle while Juliette pressed the new tube into the tyre, and when the tyre went firm and round, she spun the wheel and watched it hold its shape. It looked exactly like it had before the thorn, which felt like a small miracle.

They still missed the four o'clock showing, but Charles didn't mention it. He rode standing up on his pegs, one hand on Juliette's shoulder, as she steered them both down the hill toward home. "Faster than the bus," he shouted over the wind. She laughed and pedalled harder.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
The group chat pinged at 7:42, right as Sophie sat down to homework. She opened it expecting the usual memes. Instead Makenzie had typed: "Sophie your poster idea is so boring. we are not doing it."

Sophie's fingers accelerated across the keyboard, then stopped. She typed "wow ok," deleted it, typed "rude much," deleted that too. Arian jumped in with a shrug emoji, and someone wrote "drama." Sophie put the phone face-down on her desk and stared at her math worksheet without seeing a single number. Makenzie had been her friend since fifth grade, but lately every message came out sharp, like she was swatting people away.

At school the next morning, Sophie found Arian at the water fountain. "What is her problem?" Sophie said. "She's just mean now."

Arian wiped his mouth on his sleeve. "You know her dad lost his job last week, right? He's doing plumbing jobs for people instead. Money's really tight. She found out Tuesday."

Sophie's face went hot. "She never said anything."

"She wouldn't," Arian said. He pulled his psychology notebook out of his bag, because Ms. Janssen had just covered this exact thing in class, the unit Sophie had been absent for. He flipped to a page and held it out. "It's called the fundamental attribution error," he read. "This psychologist, Lee Ross, named it in 1977. We blame people's actions on their personality and underestimate their situation."

Sophie read the line twice. The poster comment, the swatting tone, all of it rearranged itself in her head, and she suddenly wanted to test the idea instead of just believing it. "So you're saying if I'd known about her dad, I wouldn't have thought she was a jerk."

"Basically," Arian said. "Ms. Janssen says everybody does it. She made us catch ourselves doing it all week."

That afternoon Sophie didn't text Makenzie a long explanation, because that would have been about Sophie feeling better, not about Makenzie. She walked to her house with two cookies in a bag and knocked. Makenzie opened the door a few inches, one earbud in.

"I'm not taking the poster back," Makanzie said.

"I'm not here about the poster." Sophie held up the bag. "I heard about your dad. I brought cookies. We can do your idea if you want."

Makanzie looked at the bag, then at the floor. The door swung wider. "It's a dumb idea. I only said it because I was in a bad mood."

"New plan, then," Sophie said. "But I did like your title."

Makanzie stepped back to let her in, and the smell of something burning drifted from the kitchen, where her dad was cooking dinner in his work boots.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: Prithee is a squeezed-together form of "I pray thee" and means please.
story:
The bus jolted over the pothole by the gym, and Jasmine's highlighter rolled off her script and into the aisle. Karissa lunged for it before it reached the front wheels of a backpack trolley. "You've read that same page since Maple Street," she said, handing it back.

"Because I don't get it." Jasmine turned the script toward her. Tomorrow in English they had to paraphrase a scene from Macbeth into modern English, and Ms. Tse had been clear: no summaries, actual line-by-line paraphrase, performed aloud in pairs. The words on the page sat there like a locked gate. "Fair is foul, and foul is fair" she could handle. But then the witches opened their mouths again and out came sentences that made her brain stutter.

"Read the weird part out loud," Karissa said. "Sometimes my brother reads his French that way and it untangles."

Jasmine cleared her throat, quieter than the engine. "The First Witch says, 'I'll drain him dry as hay. Sleep shall neither night nor day hang upon his penthouse lid.'" That part she could picture: the sailor staying awake, worn down. But the Second Witch had a line that had plagued her all evening. "Then she says, 'Show me, show me.'" She adjusted her grip on the page. "And the First Witch answers, 'Here I have a pilot's thumb, wrack'd as homeward he did come.' Fine, whatever. But earlier, when the witches meet the sailor's wife, the wife says something first. She yells, 'Aroint thee, witch!' And the First Witch says, 'Give me.' And the wife says, 'Prithee.'" She dropped the script on her knee. "Why would she say a nonsense word to a witch who just cursed her husband?"

August leaned over the seat behind them, because of course August had been listening. "It's not nonsense. Say it slower."

Jasmine said it slower. "Prithee." Nothing. Then she said it again, and this time she heard the pieces hiding inside it, squeezed together like fingers laced through a fence: I pray thee. "Prithee is I pray thee," she said, sitting up so fast the seatbelt buckle clattered. "It means please. She's saying please." She read the whole exchange again with that one word unlocked, and suddenly the scene flipped around. The wife wasn't just yelling at a witch. She was being polite, begging, even while the witch demanded her chestnuts. The witch wasn't strange; she was a bully taking food from someone who said please.

"So what's the modern line?" Karissa asked, holding her phone like a stopwatch. "Eight stops till school."

Jasmine thought about the woman's voice, tired, frightened, still courteous. "She'd say, 'Please, witch, I need those. My husband's already had a hard voyage.'"

"Say it like she means it."

Jasmine said it twice, and the second time it sounded like a real person. She flipped to the next speech and found "prithee" again, waiting there like a friend. Behind them, August said, "See, your witch is scared of the hag, not weird." The bus hissed to a stop at the corner, and Jasmine slid her highlighter across the row of lines she could finally read.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
The science fair board was due Monday, and Kayla was at the science centre on Saturday with a notebook, a granola bar, and no project. She had exactly one idea, salvaged from a conversation with Collin on the bus: something about the giant parabolic dishes near the entrance, the ones where you whisper into one and a person across the room hears you at the other. Nobody in her class knew why they worked. That seemed like enough to build a project on.

"You need a hypothesis," said Ava, who had come along mostly for the gift shop but was willing to be helpful for one afternoon. "Ms. Ong said that like forty times."

"I know what a hypothesis is," Kayla said. "A testable guess." What she did not say was that she had a separate problem: the big title letters for the board had already been ordered from the print shop, and they spelled WHERE HYPOTHESIS COMES FROM, because Kayla had assumed it was some boring science word that meant "a smart guess" and nothing else. The letters would arrive Sunday. There was no budget, in money or time, for a second set.

They found the dishes, two pale bowls mounted on posts about fifteen metres apart. Kayla stood at one and whispered, "Collin owes me a granola bar." At the other, a small kid repeated it to her father, who laughed. So the dishes worked. The question was what invisible thing carried the words, and Kayla's guess was that the sound bounced off the bowl shape and got aimed, like a thrown ball, straight across the room instead of spreading out.

Testing it took a while. Kayla whispered at the dish from the side, from the front, from a step to the left, while Ava stood at the far dish and reported what she heard. Off to the side, Ava heard nothing. Dead centre, clear as anything. Kayla wrote down nine trials, lined up the results, and took the median distance from the centre, the middle value when she put them in order: eleven centimetres. Anything farther than that, and the words vanished. The invisible aiming rule seemed to hold.

"It holds," Kayla said, mostly to convince herself. Then, sitting on the floor near the astronomy display, she looked up the word on the centre's little reference screen, because the board needed a definition and she wanted a proper one. She read it twice. "Ava. The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"Under what?"

"That's all it says. Putting or placing under." Kayla stared at the screen. Her ordered letters, already paid for, suddenly looked like the least boring part of the whole project. The word had been hiding a picture inside it this whole time, a foundation being slid into place beneath a guess, waiting for the experiment to check whether it could hold anything up.

The print shop closed at six. Kayla checked her phone, gathered her notebook, and started walking fast toward the exit.

"Where are you going?" Ava called.

"To tell them not to change a single letter," Kayla said.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Carter sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor with a half-finished history poster between his knees, his laptop warm on the blanket, trying to cite three sources before the project was due Monday. Simona was supposed to be helping, but she had spent the last twenty minutes typing on her phone with her shoulders up around her ears. He could hear her breathing go short and quick, the way it did before a test.

"Mr. Bighorn says the assembly Friday is mandatory," she said without looking up. "Even for kids who already turned in the permission form. I keep checking if they changed it again." Her phone buzzed and she flinched.

Carter wanted to know what was stressing her out, because if he knew, maybe he could fix it, and fixing things was what he was good at. When her phone lit up again on the carpet between them, he leaned over and picked it up to read the notification for her, the way he did with Kendrick's phone a hundred times, because Kendrick never cared.

"Give it back." Simona's voice cracked. Her hand was out, palm open, and her eyes were wet. "Please."

He handed it over at once, but the room had gone strange and stiff. She hugged the phone against her chest and stared at the poster like it had personally disappointed her. Carter's own anxiety started up in his stomach, that fluttery dropping feeling, and he realized he didn't know the rule he had just broken, only that he had broken it.

"Was it something on the screen?" he asked carefully. "I wasn't going to read your messages, I just saw it light up."

"It's not about the screen." She wiped her face with her sleeve. "A boundary is a limit I set about what I'm comfortable with. Like how people treat me, or touch my stuff, or use my things without asking. You picked up my phone without asking. Kendrick might not mind, but I do." She said it flat, not mean, the way she corrected his math.

So it was a rule that changed from person to person, and the only way to know it was to ask first. Carter tested the idea right there. "Okay. Can I see the notification, if you show it to me yourself? You don't have to explain it."

Simona looked at him for a long second, then turned the screen around. It was her mom, reminding her to pack her epinephrine injector because her little brother's birthday party would have cake with peanuts in it, and her allergy was serious. That was all. All that shaking over cake. She laughed a wet little laugh, and some of the tightness went out of her shoulders.

They finished the poster, and it came out good, the timeline neat and the citations in the right places. But at the door, Simona paused with her backpack on one shoulder. "I'm still kind of embarrassed I cried over nothing," she said. Carter didn't tell her it wasn't nothing, because that would be deciding for her what her limit was, and he was done doing that. He just held the door and said, "Text me when you get home. Or don't. Your call." She smiled, but it was smaller than usual, and she was still typing something into her phone as she went down the steps.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
Evan had been waiting three weeks for the microscope lab, and now that it had finally arrived, his slide looked like nothing. He squinted into the eyepiece, twisted the fine focus, and saw only a pale grey blur that smelled faintly of onion even through the glass. Across the lab table, Shae was tapping her pencil against her notebook in a rhythm that would have been annoying if it were not so exactly the beat of the song stuck in his own head. "Yours working?" he asked. "Mine's a smudge."

"Mine's better than working," Shae said. "Mine's broken in the interesting way. Come look." She slid her chair over so fast it squeaked, and Evan took her place at the scope. What he saw made him forget his own blur entirely. The field was full of neat rectangles, row after row of them, stacked like bricks in a wall. "I think I put my slide in upside down and now it's showing the wall of the building," Shae said. "Or a picture of a brick wall. That would be a weird thing to print on a cover slip."

Evan did not laugh, even though the image of a tiny printed brick wall was honestly funny, because something about it snagged in his mind. He turned the fine focus one click. The rectangles sharpened, and inside each one he could make out a small dark dot near the edge, like a pebble pressed into every single brick. Brick walls did not have identical pebbles in every brick. Neither did photographs of walls. "Wait," he said slowly. "What if each brick is one cell? Then the thick outside border around every rectangle is the cell wall, and that's why they look like rows of bricks." Shae leaned in, looked, went quiet for a moment, and then let out a groan. "I wrote 'brick wall' on my diagram. In pen."

Fixing it was tedious. Shae carefully crossed out her label, added an amendment in the margin ("not a wall, cells, sorry"), and then had to relabel the thin inner line as the membrane and the dark dot as the nucleus, which took her twice as long because her handwriting got smaller when she was embarrassed. Evan stayed beside her instead of rushing back to his own blurry slide, mostly because he wanted to keep looking at hers, but also because she had gone quiet in a way that meant she needed a witness who was not going to tease her. "It's not a mistake anyone else caught," he said. "Brooklynn drew hers as a honeycomb, and Marcus thinks his is a snake scale." From two tables over, Brooklynn's head popped up. "It is a honeycomb," she insisted, then looked into her eyepiece again and said, "Oh. No. Those are cells."

Then Evan had an idea about his own slide. If Shae's onion cells had shown up so clearly, maybe his problem was not the microscope but the piece of skin he had chosen, a thick fold from the curved outside of the onion instead of the papery thin layer Ms. Bélanger had demonstrated. He peeled again, this time hunting for the thinnest, almost transparent shred, and dropped it onto a fresh slide with one drop of stain. To prolong the suspense for himself, he counted to five before bending to the eyepiece. Focus, one slow turn, and there they were: row after row of bricks, each one with its dark little nucleus, waiting to be labeled. He heard Shae laugh beside him and felt her tap his shoulder. "Told you it was the good kind of broken," she said, and slid him her pen.
